newsitem.title: USA: Army sergeant pleads guilty in Mo. assault case.
newsitem.headline: Army sergeant pleads guilty in Mo. assault case.

text.p: A drill sergeant at an Army training base pleaded guilty Thursday to charges of assault and abuse at the Fort Leonard Wood training base in Missouri, an official said.

In a court martial at the base, Staff Sgt. Anthony Fore admitted he put his hands around the necks of trainees and touched female recruits' breasts. He faces possible imprisonment and dishonourable discharge at his sentencing, expected soon.

Meanwhile, officials said more than 100 reports of sexual harassment at the Army's Aberdeen Proving Ground in Maryland had been referred for investigation and the number of soldiers implicated may increase beyond the 20 already disclosed.

Large increases in the number charged was unlikely, said spokesman Ed Starnes of the base's training facility, where the scandal erupted in November. Some 6,250 calls to an Army sexual harassment hotline were received as of Thursday, and 850 cases were "deemed to warrant further investigation," of which 121 were from the proving ground, Starnes said.

An official at Fort Leonard Wood said Fore was charged in August with failing to obey a general regulation, indecent assault, maltreatment and assault and battery. The Army said the charges resulted from an ongoing investigation into trainees' complaints but were not related to the rape and sexual harassment probe in Maryland.

Another soldier at the Missouri base, Staff Sgt. Loren Taylor, was discharged, demoted and sentenced to confinement last month after he admitted to having sex with three female recruits. Army regulations forbid all sexual relationships between commanders and subordinates.

A total of 20 soldiers have been publicly implicated at Aberdeen, including three trainers arraigned last week and facing trial next year, 15 who were suspended from their duties pending investigation and two who were fined.

Army investigators had almost finished screening interviews of nearly 1,000 female recruits who had attended the Aberdeen training facility since January 1995, Starnes said. Additional charges could be filed as investigators focus on cases identified in the screenings, he said.

He said any additional charges would be made in a group rather than one-by-one. "I think the number of suspects will settle down and then victims will clear up, starting pretty soon ... There could be some (charges) next week, it could be in a month," Starnes said.

"I would not see it expanding greatly -- 20 to 25 (total). That's just an educated guess," he said. He said an initial screening phase of the investigation was winding down and additional charges could be filed.
